newsitem.title: JAPAN: East Asian buyers give USDA report mixed reception.
newsitem.headline: East Asian buyers give USDA report mixed reception.

text.p: East Asian soy buyers gave a mixed reception on Wednesday to a key overnight report from the USDA that unexpectedly revealed it was maintaining its 1996/97 soybean ending stocks estimate unchanged at 140 million bushels.

Chicago soybean futures fell on the news as the trade had been predicting the USDA would trim its stock figure to between 125-130 million bushels, giving a further upward twist to U.S. prices, which hit a 8-1/2 year peak on Monday.
"We had our crisis management team in place before the USDA report, but the number simply spelled comfort," Taiwan Hui Shung Group soybean buyer Jack Lee told Reuters.

While Taiwanese buyers were cheered by the numbers and South Korean dealers said weak fundamentals should trigger a further correction in soybean and soy product prices, Japanese traders were apprehensive of another blistering rally.
They urged Japanese edible oil suppliers, who have recently raised domestic prices, to quicken their purchases of U.S. soybeans.
"Despite Tuesday's price falls, we basically assume the CBOT (Chicago Board of Trade) will rise further," a soybean trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.

He pointed to U.S. traders' comments on the resilience of CBOT futures overnight, where the benchmark May contract ended weaker on the USDA news at $8.55-1/2 a bushel, but still well off the day's lows and not far off Monday's 8-1/2 year high of $8.62 a bushel.
Japanese soybean crushers have been squeezed by a combination of the rally in Chicago prices and the yen's sharp fall against the U.S. dollar since late last year.
The dollar rose to about 125 yen to the dollar in February from around 113 yen in mid-December, 1996.
"These two factors will increasingly damage their profit margins, and pressure them to raise product prices," one trader commented.
Nisshin Oil Mills Ltd, Japan's largest edible oil maker, said it had raised edible oil prices for hotels and restaurants by nearly seven percent, starting from February deliveries.
Other edible oil manufacturers are almost sure to follow, traders said.
The gloom among Japanese soy buyers has not, however, spread to Taiwan or South Korea.
Analysts in Taiwan said soybean futures' technical indicators were still trending mostly higher, but warned they could turn quickly if small funds started profit-taking.
"Small funds' profit-taking will drag the indicators down," a Taipei analyst said.

In South Korea, traders said prices may also be pressured by a USDA estimate that U.S. soybean exports could experience a record fall in the second-half of this marketing year due to competition from bumper harvests in South America.
They added that CBOT soybean futures remain heavily overbought despite Tuesday's retreat with the contract's nine-day relative strength index (RSI) at 81.19, down only slightly from Monday's 85.44.
"In the short term, soybeans will face a correction to ease the highly overbought situation," one Seoul-based trader said.
South Korean edible oil processors are seen shrugging off current volatile prices and proceeding with purchases of 50,000 tonnes of U.S. soybean for shipment in April, traders said.

South Korea's soybean imports in 1996 totalled 1,465,000 tonnes, down slightly from 1,468,000 tonnes the previous year. Japanese trade houses said they are to send a mission to Beijing later this week to negotiate with Chinese suppliers over soybean exports to Japan for the May-September 1997 period.
Japan imported 157,796 tonnes of soybeans from China during 1996, Finance Ministry data showed. Chinese soybeans are mainly used for making miso or soybean paste.
The Japanese are expected to ask Chinese suppliers to keep soybean prices unchanged from the January-April period at nearly US$395 a tonne on an FOB basis, traders said.
But the Chinese are unlikely to accomodate the request and will probably aim to raise their levels on the back of the surge in world prices, they said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
